extracted.intended_audience: general readers of classic folktales and students of literature
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and interpreting prescriptive statements, maxims, and behavioral standards embedded in a translated folktale (Vikram and the Vampire). Focuses on social, moral, and practical advice the narrative voices give. Useful for literary analysis or adapting moralizing elements in creative writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parenting mistakes: over-vigilance and under-vigilance
rubrics_metrics.description: “O king! men commit two capital mistakes in rearing the ‘domestic calamity,’ and these are over-vigilance and under-vigilance.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: Over-vigilance (never losing sight of daughters, showing suspicion) can incite evil-doing; under-vigilance (taking no trouble, permitting idleness and wicked company) breeds opportunity for vice. Anti-patterns: obvious suspicion that provokes rebellion; total neglect leaving children idle and exposed to bad influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor parental treatment to a child's character
rubrics_metrics.description: “The wise will study the characters of their children, and modify their treatment accordingly. If a daughter be naturally good, she will be treated with a prudent confidence. If she be vicious, an apparent trust will be reposed in her; but her father and mother will secretly ever be upon their guard.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Observe individual disposition and adopt different outward policies (prudent confidence vs apparent trust) combined with inward vigilance for safety. Example: giving liberty to the good, covert supervision of the wicked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical traits and implied moral/esthetic judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions of Jayashri: “Her fine large eyes had heavy and rather full eyelids, which are to be avoided. Her hands were symmetrical... her mouth was somewhat underhung; and her voice was so deep, that at times it sounded like that of a man.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit rule: certain physical features are flagged as undesirable or morally suggestive in the narrator's cultural aesthetics. Use as a guideline for character description: enumerate specific features and their narrative valence (to be avoided, neutral, or praiseworthy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Beautiful woman is more virtuous than the ugly (narrative claim)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Yet must I confess, continued the parrot, that, as a rule, the beautiful woman is more virtuous than the ugly.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justification offered: beauty's vanity and conceit can help resist temptation; ugliness must tempt and so may yield. This is an asserted generalization used to explain character behavior—treat as a cultural trope rather than empirical rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Women’s three emotional states toward masters (love, hate, indifference)
rubrics_metrics.description: “You see, my king! there are three several states of feeling with which women regard their masters, and these are love, hate, and indifference. Of all, love is the weakest and the most transient... Hate ... will easily become ... love; and hate-love may perhaps last a little longer than love-love.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance for plotting or character interaction: these three states can be narratively permuted; a skilled agent (here, described as 'man versed in the Lila Shastra') can turn indifference into hate, then into love. Antipattern: assuming feelings are fixed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Love as divine abnegation (parrot’s moral view)
rubrics_metrics.description: “For truly he loved her... there is something holy in such love. It becomes not only a faith, but the best of faiths—an abnegation of self which emancipates the spirit from its straightest and earthliest bondage...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This presents an idealized, religious conception of love as self-renunciation and spiritual elevation. Use when portraying sanctified, sacrificial love in characters or moralizing narration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Love as mania and selfishness (Baital’s counterview)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Love is, according to me, somewhat akin to mania, a temporary condition of selfishness, a transient confusion of identity... Ye call love a spell, an alchemy, a deity. Why? Because it deifies self by gratifying all man’s pride... under the mask of complete unegotism.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasting critical perspective: depict love as self-deception and ego-gratification. Use to create ironic, skeptical, or cynical narratorial tones and to characterize narrators who distrust romantic idealism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test servants by obedience, not words
rubrics_metrics.description: “To try thy servant, bid him do things in season and out of season: if he obey thee willingly, know him to be useful; if he reply, dismiss him at once.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical criterion for evaluating loyalty and usefulness: obedience under varied commands is the test. Example in text: Birbal’s willing nightly guard duty marks him as trustworthy. Anti-pattern: trusting mere profession or talk without trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merit and practical innovation in military command
rubrics_metrics.description: Rajeshwar’s reforms: he “consulted chiefly his own experience and judgment... threw aside the systematic plans... displayed a skill in the choice of ground, in the use of light troops, and in securing his own supplies whilst he cut off those of the enemy... Finding that the bows of his troops were clumsy... he had them all changed... he also gave his attention to the sword handles... organized a special corps of warriors using fire arrows...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules for effective command: favor empirical judgment over rote tradition; modernize equipment; value mobility and logistics; promote based on battlefield merit rather than seniority. Examples: replacing clumsy bows, creating specialized corps, dismissing incapable aged officers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer merit over seniority in promotions
rubrics_metrics.description: Rajeshwar refused obsolete senior captains, “rendered the honour valuable by conferring it only upon the deserving,” and raised men who distinguished themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: award rank and honors only to deserving performers; avoid blanket rewards that devalue distinction. Narrative example: rapid military success after meritocratic reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self‑valuation as social signaling
rubrics_metrics.description: “Set a high price upon yourselves, and each man shall say to his neighbour, ‘In this man there must be something.’ Tell everyone that you are brave, clever, generous, or even handsome, and after a time they will begin to believe you.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical rule for reputation management: confident self-presentation shapes others' beliefs. Use as guidance for characters cultivating social standing or for dialog about self-fashioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charitable distribution and public service as use of wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: Birbal’s use of wealth: “He used every morning to divide it into two portions, one of which was distributed to Brahmans and Parohitas. Of the remaining moiety... he gave one as alms to pilgrims... With the remaining fourth... he regaled the poor, while he himself and his family ate what was left.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescriptive model for handling sudden wealth: structured distribution to religious/classes in need and provision for the poor; juxtaposed with personal service (guard duty) to demonstrate devotion. Use as a template for virtuous or performative charity in character actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test claims by demonstration, not rhetoric
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrated when Birbal, asked to prove skill, “put forth his left hand... waved his blade... and, with a dexterous stroke, so shaved off a bit of nail that it fell to the ground, and not a drop of blood appeared upon the finger-tip.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule: verify competence through practical test or demonstration. Narrative use: a simple feat can settle disputes over ability; anti-pattern is accepting grandiose verbal claims without proof.
